ADR momentum and potential SOX inclusion
ADR momentum: An additional driver alongside structural growth
On Mar. 24, SK Hynix announced that it had confidentially filed a registration statement with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) for a potential ADR listing. It is targeting a listing within 2026, although details such as the offering size and structure have yet to be finalized. We expect the ADR listing to serve as a positive share catalyst.
The firm has retired all treasury shares not held for employee compensation purposes as of Feb. 9, while recent revisions to the Commercial Act have tightened restrictions on treasury share disposals. Accordingly, we believe new share issuance is the most likely mechanism for the ADR offering. Because SK Square, the firm’s largest shareholder with a 20.5% stake, must retain ownership of at least 20% to maintain its holding company status, the size of the new issuance is likely to be capped at around 2.5% of the current share count.
Assuming a maximum issuance of 2.5% of shares outstanding (17.8mn shares) and based on the current share price and USD/KRW rate (1,500), the offering size would start at approximately US$27.7bn. And with foreign investor bookbuilding, the market cap could expand even further. At that size, SK Hynix would rank around 25th among the 30 constituents of the PHLX Semiconductor Sector Index (SOX), making future inclusion a real possibility.
To qualify for SOX inclusion, a stock must have been listed for at least six months and maintain monthly trading volume of at least 1.5mn shares. This would correspond to roughly 10% of shares assumed under our maximum issuance scenario. For the current 30 constituents, daily trading volume averages 2.2% of shares outstanding, suggesting that achieving 10% monthly share turnover should not be particularly challenging. If listed by end-2026, SK Hynix could be considered for inclusion during the Sep. 2027 rebalancing.
The key benefits of inclusion are higher valuation potential and passive fund inflows. Notably, the index caps the weights of its top three constituents at 12%, 10%, and 8%, while limiting all remaining names to 4%. Thus, when the prices of the top three constituents rise, passive inflows can spill over to lower-weighted index members.
Deeply undervalued relative to SOX
Our operating profit forecasts for 2Q26 and 2026 stand at W67tr and W290tr, respectively, above the consensus (W64tr and W256tr, respectively). The stock is currently trading at a 2027F P/E of 5.2x and P/B of 2.5x, well below the SOX averages of 36.7x and 11.2x, respectively. We reiterate our target price of W3,800,000.

Additional upside from large-scale shareholder returns
Shareholder returns: An additional driver alongside structural growth
Samsung Electronics (SEC) operates under a three-year shareholder return framework, returning 50% of cumulative free cash flow (FCF) generated over each three-year period. Under the current (2024-26) program, the company pays an annual base dividend of W9.8tr (approximately W30tr over three years) and pays a special dividend if FCF exceeds its target. With 2026 marking the final year of the current cycle, a special dividend payout appears likely given the likelihood of excess FCF generation.
That said, uncertainty remains regarding the treatment of M&A spending in the FCF calculation. Under the 2018?20 shareholder return policy, cash outflows related to M&As were explicitly excluded from FCF calculations. However, this exclusion clause was removed starting with the 2021?23 framework. Accordingly, we consider multiple scenarios based on shareholder return method (cash dividends vs. share buybacks/cancellations) and the treatment of M&A spending in FCF calculations.
Assuming a minimum payout ratio of 25%―the threshold required to qualify for separate taxation of dividend income―we estimate shareholder returns under four scenarios: 100% cash dividends (scenario 1); 70% cash dividends and 30% share buybacks/cancellations (scenario 2); and M&A scenarios that differ in whether related spending is deducted from FCF (scenarios 3 and 4). Based on these scenarios, we estimate dividend yields at 3.7?6.5% for common shares and 5.8?10.1% for preferred shares (based on the current share price).
These dividend yield levels should provide solid downside support for shares. In addition, preferred shares are currently trading at a 36% discount to common shares, which is excessive compared to the historical average of 22%. Considering that the discount narrowed to as low as 5% ahead of the Mar. 2021 special dividend resolution, investors should watch for a potential narrowing of the preferred share discount ahead of the anticipated special dividend resolution in Mar. 2027.
Moreover, we believe SEC is highly likely to increase base dividends starting next year. The fixed annual dividend of W9.6?9.8tr over the past nine years has been based on returning 50% of three-year cumulative FCF of around W60tr. From 2026 onward, however, annual FCF is likely to exceed W200tr. As such, we expect either an increase in the fixed dividend or a higher FCF return ratio.
Undervalued based on earnings fundamentals alone
We forecast operating profit at W89tr for 2Q26 and W371tr for 2026, higher than the consensus estimates of W88tr and W352tr, respectively. The stock is currently trading at 2026F and 2027F P/Es of 6.9x and 5x, respectively, and 2026F and 2027F P/Bs of 2.8x and 1.9x, respectively. We maintain our target price of W550,000, which corresponds to a 2026F P/E of 12x.
